title: Opening, form and publication
short: An epitaph-elegy in two quatrains of common metre, first printed in Landor's Simonidea (1806).
body: 'What avails' means 'what is the use of' (OED, 'avail'). The rhetorical question is the classical consolation formula turned upside down: rank, beauty, virtue and grace are of no avail against death. The poem is in common (hymnal) metre, alternating eight- and six-syllable lines rhyming abab cdcd. Simonidea, the 1806 collection, was named after the Greek poet Simonides, famed for epitaphs, which suggests how Landor wanted his elegies read: in the compressed, lapidary manner of Greek inscriptions. The text here follows Landor's later collected Works (1846).

title: the sceptred race
short: A noble lineage; Rose Aylmer was the daughter of Henry, fourth Baron Aylmer.
body: 'Sceptred' (bearing a sceptre, royal) is used loosely for aristocratic descent. Compare John of Gaunt's 'This royal throne of kings, this sceptred isle' (Richard II 2.1.40). The phrase means 'what is the use of noble birth', and it is the first of four gifts (birth, beauty, virtue, grace) that the poem lists only to cancel. The Aylmer barony belonged to the peerage of Ireland. The opening thus begins with the most worldly of the gifts and moves towards the spiritual.

title: the form divine
short: Her beauty, almost godlike; the inversion echoes Milton's 'human face divine'.
body: Milton, lamenting his blindness, lists what he can no longer see: 'Or flocks, or herds, or human face divine' (Paradise Lost III.44). Landor's inverted 'form divine' borrows the cadence and the sense of loss. The adjective after the noun gives the line a Latin or Greek formality appropriate to an epitaph. Milton's line, from the invocation to light, is itself a lament for what cannot be seen again, which suits Landor's later 'May weep, but never see'.

title: every virtue, every grace
short: Moral goodness and charm of manner; 'grace' may also suggest the classical Graces and divine grace.
body: The paired 'every' generalizes praise in the manner of eighteenth-century epitaphs. 'Grace' covers elegance of manner and movement and, by association, the three Graces of classical myth; it can also suggest the Christian sense of divine favour, so that the line ends the catalogue on spiritual as well as social gifts. Line 4 then gathers all four into the name: 'Rose Aylmer, all were thine.'

title: Rose Aylmer (1779-1800)
short: Rose Whitworth Aylmer, a young aristocrat Landor knew in South Wales; she died of cholera in Calcutta on 2 March 1800, aged twenty.
body: Landor met her around 1796-97 in South Wales (he was living at Swansea). She lent him Clara Reeve's The Progress of Romance (1785), in which he found the tale that became his poem Gebir (1798). After her mother's remarriage she went to India in 1798 with her aunt, Lady Russell, wife of Sir Henry Russell, and died there of cholera. She was buried in the South Park Street Cemetery, Calcutta, where her tomb still stands. The archive's headnote says she died in Wales; the records place her death in Calcutta.

title: the repeated name
short: The name ends the first stanza and begins the second, a repetition (anadiplosis) like a mourner calling it aloud.
body: Repeating the final words of one unit at the start of the next is the figure called anadiplosis. Here it bridges the two stanzas and turns the close of the eulogy into the start of the lament. The name, with its soft liquids and long vowels, is the music of the poem; in October 1831 Henry Crabb Robinson told Landor that Lamb, drunk or sober, was ever muttering 'Rose Aylmer'.

sources.cite: E. V. Lucas, The Life of Charles Lamb, vol. 2 (1905)

title: these wakeful eyes / May weep, but never see
short: Sleepless eyes that can weep for her but never see her again, both because she is dead and because she died far away in India.
body: 'Wakeful' prepares the night of vigil in line 7. The contrast of weeping and seeing makes the eyes the instrument of both loss and mourning. Landor had not seen her since she sailed for India, so the line holds two separations, of distance and of death. In November 1831 he told Crabb Robinson, half joking, that he had written the poem while cleaning his teeth before bed, but added that the night of sorrow had really been devoted to her.

title: A night of memories and of sighs / I consecrate
short: He dedicates a whole night to her memory, as one dedicates something holy; the poem itself is that offering.
body: To 'consecrate' (Latin consecrare, to make sacred) is to set apart for a religious purpose (OED). The night of memories and sighs is an offering like those made at a tomb in classical epitaph. Charles Lamb, writing to Landor in 1832, said the poem had 'a charm I cannot explain' and that he 'lived upon it for weeks'. Its fame rests on this restraint: eight short lines with no image of her, only the name and the vow.
